title: Intermittent gateway latency
executive_summary: INC-010 (SEV3, intermittent api-gateway latency, reported 2026-09-29 19:51Z, symptom start 19:45Z) is classified INCONCLUSIVE. The root cause could not be established. The only clear signal is a rise in api-gateway p99 latency from a stable baseline of about 253 ms to a window mean of 341 ms (max 557 ms), with onset at 19:40Z (met-api-gateway-p99_latency_ms-1930-2010). The rise is thin: only two elevated samples, and 24 of 41 gateway points are missing from 19:50Z onward, so persistence is unknown. p95 rose only about 8% (met-api-gateway-p95_latency_ms-1930-2010). Error rate, timeout rate, CPU, memory and request rate were flat (met-api-gateway-cpu_pct-1930-1955). No deployments or configuration changes were found between 18:30Z and 20:10Z. No leading hypothesis is selected. Candidate explanations remain open: a telemetry or ingestion artefact (H2, confidence 0.15), an unidentified upstream dependency slowdown (H1, confidence 0.12), and a short non-sustained tail event or measurement artefact (H3, confidence 0.07). The large-upload saturation hypothesis (H4) is rejected.

The true service latency is unknown. Mechanism: A collector or ingestion fault starting at 19:35Z drops or delays metric points for several services. Gateway tail percentiles computed from partial samples may be inflated, or the gateway pipeline may share the fault and lose samples from 19:50Z.

critic_review.summary: Gateway P99 does rise from a stable ~253 ms baseline to 337 ms at 19:40 and 557 ms at 19:45, and the onset is consistent across the query windows. However, the signal is thin: only two elevated samples, with 24 of 41 gateway points missing from 19:50 onward, so persistence is unknown. P95 rises only modestly (~7%), while error rate, timeout rate, CPU, memory and request rate are flat. No deployments or config changes were found from 18:30 to 20:10Z. No upstream latency data covers 19:35-19:50Z for auth, order, payment or user, so H1's specific upstream cannot be identified and H1 remains an untested category-level guess. The upstream metric gaps starting at 19:35Z are a shared boundary that H2 links to a telemetry fault, but gateway data was present across that boundary, so H2 is not established. H4 is contradicted by flat CPU, memory and request rate and by a recurring one-off upload WARN with no latency effect. Further evidence is unlikely to be obtainable in this final round, since the upstream and collector data the tools expose are missing for the critical window.

assessments.reasoning: Gateway tail rise at 19:40-19:45 is real and tail-only, but no upstream latency evidence exists for the window, so the culprit upstream and the causal link are unsupported. Persistence beyond 19:45 is unobserved.
Shared upstream gap starting 19:35 is noted, but gateway P99 is present across that boundary, and no collector health counters are available to test distortion. Not accepted.

Artefact or transient explanation fits the thin two-sample signal and the missing post-19:45 data, but the 19:25-19:35 baseline is stable and the jump is large (+35% to +120%). Cannot be distinguished without post-19:50 data.
CPU flat (34.6% vs 34.7%), request rate flat (-2.3%), memory within normal range, and the identical slow-upload WARN at 18:54Z produced no latency shift. Strong contradiction.

corrective_actions: Keep the incident open at SEV3 and confirm in real time whether api-gateway p99 is still elevated; if it is, escalate. Treat this as a user-impact investigation, not a confirmed regression.
Check api-gateway p99 and p95 directly from raw request traces or access logs rather than the aggregated metric, to rule out a sampling artefact in the partial window (affects H2/H3).
Pull per-upstream latency (auth, order, payment, user) for 19:35Z to 19:50Z from the service's own telemetry source, since the metric store has no data for that window. This is needed to test H1.

Recover or re-query the telemetry-collector and ingestion pipeline data for 19:35Z to 19:50Z. The service name was not recognised by the log tool, so a different identifier or direct collector health check is needed.
preventive_actions: Add per-upstream latency metrics for api-gateway's dependencies (auth, order, payment, user) with a consistent label set, so future tail-latency incidents can be attributed to a specific upstream.
Add a health or freshness metric for the telemetry pipeline (collector drop counts, ingestion lag, missing-point rate) so telemetry gaps are detected and do not look like service behaviour.

Define a p99 alert on api-gateway that requires a sustained breach (for example, several consecutive evaluation windows) and reports data completeness alongside the value, to avoid acting on thin or partial samples.
Make the log query tooling cover the telemetry collector and all services that take part in gateway traffic, so evidence gaps of this kind can be closed in future investigations.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on api-gateway p99 above roughly 1.5x the 253 ms baseline for 3 or more consecutive windows, and show the count of missing points in the same panel.
Monitor api-gateway p95 and error/timeout rate together with p99, so a tail-only rise is seen in context.
Add dashboards for auth, order, payment and user p99 and p95 at the same resolution as the gateway, with a missing-data indicator.
Monitor telemetry collector health: dropped points, ingestion lag and scrape failures, with an alert on any gap longer than 5 minutes.
Log upload size and request duration for requests above 1 MB at the gateway, so that the one-off upload WARN can be correlated with latency if it recurs.
limitations: The root cause is not established. No leading hypothesis is selected, and all candidates remain at low confidence (0.07 to 0.15).
